prompt: Some readers believe that once you start a book, you should finish it, even if you are not enjoying it, because books often get better and stopping becomes a habit. Others believe it is fine to put a book down and choose another, because time spent reading something you dislike can make you stop reading at all. Which view do you agree with? Support your position with examples from your own reading.
guidance: A strong response takes a side and explains what is gained or lost either way: patience and surprise against time and interest. Credit a writer who uses a specific book they finished or abandoned, with what happened, and who answers the best point of the other view. Naming many titles earns nothing by itself; one well-explained example is stronger.
accessibility_note: Any reading counts, including assigned books, comics, series or articles, so the prompt does not reward students with large home libraries.

prompt: Write about a time you taught someone how to do something, such as a game, a recipe, a skill or a school task. What did you have to figure out in order to explain it well, and what did teaching it show you about the thing you were teaching?
guidance: A strong response tells one teaching episode in order, with the moment the explanation first failed and what the writer changed. The best essays notice something they understood only by explaining it. An essay that lists everything the writer knows about the topic without the person being taught is underdeveloped; the other person's confusion is the engine of the story.
accessibility_note: Teaching a younger sibling, a friend or an adult how to use a phone feature all count, so every student has an example; the skill taught need not be impressive.

prompt: Some people would rather have a small circle of companions they know deeply. Others would rather know a large number of people more casually, from many different places. Which kind of social life seems more valuable to you, and why? Support your position with specific examples from your own life, your reading or your observation.
guidance: A strong response defines what it means by "close" and argues from what each kind of friendship actually provides: who you call in a bad week, who introduces you to new things. Credit a writer who handles the obvious objection to their own side. Personal examples should be specific moments rather than descriptions of personality.
accessibility_note: Students who feel they have few friends can argue for either side from observation or reading, and the prompt never asks anyone to count or describe their own friendships in detail.

prompt: Some people believe that the best way to learn about the past is to read books written by historians. Others believe you learn more by listening to older relatives or neighbors describe what they lived through. Which way of learning about the past do you think teaches more? Support your position with specific examples.
guidance: A strong response weighs what each source is good at: a historian can compare many accounts, while a person who was there can give detail no book has. Credit a writer who recognizes a weakness of their preferred source (a memory can be mistaken; a book can be distant) and explains why their choice still teaches more. One concrete example of something learned either way is worth more than general praise of history.
accessibility_note: A student without older relatives nearby can draw on a teacher, a neighbor, a recorded interview or a memoir they have read, so no particular family situation is assumed.

prompt: Describe an object you own that would not be worth much money to anyone else but matters a great deal to you. Explain where it came from, what it reminds you of, and why you have kept it.
guidance: A strong response makes the object visible with precise detail and then lets its meaning come from a story: where it came from or a moment it was part of. The importance should be explained, not just asserted. An essay that lists several objects, or that describes the object without ever saying why it matters, is underdeveloped.
accessibility_note: The prompt asks for something of little money value on purpose, so a ticket stub, a drawing, a stone or a worn-out piece of clothing is as strong a choice as anything, and no student is disadvantaged by what their family can afford.

prompt: Some people believe that arriving on time is a basic sign of respect, even among close friends. Others believe that being a few minutes late is no big deal when people know each other well. Which view do you agree with, and why? Support your position with examples from your own experience or observation.
guidance: A strong response draws a clear line and explains the reasoning behind it, for example whether the cost of lateness falls on the person kept waiting. Credit a writer who considers where the line moves (a school bus, a movie, a friend's house) and uses one remembered incident in detail. An essay that simply says lateness is rude or that friends do not mind is thin.
accessibility_note: Every student has waited for someone or been waited for, so the prompt requires no particular experience, and either position can be argued well.

prompt: Write about a time you were part of a group that disagreed about what to do, such as a team, a club, a class project or a family plan. Explain what the disagreement was about, how it was settled, and whether you think it was settled in the best way.
guidance: A strong response explains both sides of the disagreement fairly before telling how it ended. The best essays judge the outcome: was the decision good, was the process fair, would the writer handle it differently now? An essay that only narrates who said what, without any evaluation, is underdeveloped.
accessibility_note: A family deciding where to eat or what to watch is as valid as a team or club, so students without organized activities have an example.

prompt: Some people believe the best way to celebrate a birthday or a holiday is with a big gathering of family and friends. Others prefer to spend the day quietly with just one or two people. Which way of celebrating do you think is better? Support your position with specific examples from your own experience or observation.
guidance: A strong response explains what each kind of celebration gives and costs, for example the energy of a crowd against the attention of a few people, and ties the choice to one remembered celebration. Credit a writer who admits when the other way would be better. An essay that only lists what happened at a party, without arguing, is underdeveloped.
accessibility_note: The prompt asks which way of celebrating is better, not what the writer has had, so a student whose celebrations have been small or simple, or whose family does not mark birthdays or holidays, can argue from a celebration they attended, saw or read about; any tradition counts.
